items.subject: RC
items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Barnacles are the toughest animals to be found anywhere along a rocky shore at low tide.
choices.B: Tide pool animals are built to survive swings in heat and salt that the open sea never brings.
choices.C: Tide pools are calm, protected places where small sea creatures stay safe from the harsh ocean.
choices.D: Sudden rainstorms are the most serious threat facing ocean animals nearly everywhere in the world.

items.explanation: The passage lists the pools' fast swings in temperature and salt, shows the animals' equipment for meeting them, and ends by calling them “specialists in a kind of hardship.” The choice calling the pools calm and protected is exactly the comfortable idea the third paragraph exists to correct, and the choice about barnacles offers one animal as the whole point. Strategy: choose the choice that covers the whole passage, not one example.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: The barnacle is one of three animals the passage uses as an example, and it never says one shore animal is tougher than another; the question asks what the whole passage is about.
why.C: The pools only look peaceful from a distance, and the last paragraph says plainly that the pool is the harsher place.
why.D: A rainstorm is one of the fast swings a pool animal has to meet, and the passage says nothing in the open ocean changes that quickly.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: According to the passage, how do sea stars avoid the worst of the sun?

choices.A: They swim out into deeper water and wait there until the tide returns.
choices.B: They travel back to a shallow groove worn into the rock.
choices.C: They pull a set of hard plates shut over their soft bodies.
choices.D: They slide under ledges and into cracks the light cannot reach.

items.explanation: The second paragraph states that when the sun is high, sea stars slide under ledges and into cracks the light cannot reach. Pulling hard plates shut belongs to the barnacle, and travelling back to a worn groove belongs to the limpet. Strategy: check that the detail belongs to the animal the question names.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: No pool animal leaves for deeper water in this passage; the fish from twenty meters down is the one carried in, and it would not last an afternoon.
why.B: Traveling back to a worn groove is what the limpet does, and the question asks about the sea stars.
why.C: The hard plates belong to the barnacle, which shuts them to trap a little seawater; the question asks how the sea stars get out of the sun.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The passage suggests that a limpet travels back to its own groove before the water leaves because

choices.A: other limpets are unable to reach that part of the rock at all.
choices.B: the rock inside the groove stays cooler than any other place on the shore.
choices.C: its shell seals tightly against the worn stone and keeps water in.
choices.D: the groove holds bits of food that the limpet has stored there for later.

items.explanation: The paragraph is about equipment for staying wet — the barnacle traps a reserve of seawater — and it says the limpet's shell fits the worn stone tightly, which is what the return trip buys. The choice about cooler rock borrows the sea star's shade, which the passage never connects to the groove. Strategy: combine two nearby facts rather than making a leap.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: The passage never has limpets competing for space on the rock; what matters about the groove is that this limpet's own shell fits it.
why.B: Shade is how the sea stars escape the high sun, and the passage never says the groove is any cooler than the rock around it.
why.D: Months of feeding are how the groove got worn, but the passage never says the limpet keeps food there; it returns because its shell fits the worn stone tightly.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: In the second paragraph, *reserve* most nearly means

choices.A: a store kept back for later use.
choices.B: a quiet, shy way of behaving around others.
choices.C: an order for a seat placed ahead of time.
choices.D: a wild area set aside to protect animals.

items.explanation: The barnacle traps seawater “enough to keep its body damp until the ocean comes back,” so the reserve is a store saved for later. The protected-area meaning is a real sense of the word and the one a nature passage invites, but a barnacle's shell is not a wildlife preserve. Strategy: test each dictionary meaning inside the actual sentence.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: That is a real meaning of the word, but what the barnacle traps inside its plates is seawater, and water is a thing rather than a way of behaving.
why.C: That is the meaning you get from booking a seat ahead of time; here the barnacle is keeping enough seawater to stay damp until the ocean comes back.
why.D: That is a nature reserve, the meaning a passage about sea animals invites; here the reserve is the small amount of seawater a barnacle traps inside its plates.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The third paragraph mainly serves to

choices.A: correct a comfortable idea about tide pools and say what the pools really demand.
choices.B: offer one more example of the special equipment a shore animal carries.
choices.C: explain how fish from deep water are collected and studied by scientists.
choices.D: describe how the pools look to someone standing at a distance from the shore.

items.explanation: It opens “It would be a mistake to picture a tide pool as a gentler ocean” and ends by calling the pool the harsher place. The choices about another animal's equipment and about the view from a distance describe the two paragraphs before it, not this one. Strategy: ask what a paragraph does to the ones around it, not only what it mentions.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: The animals' equipment is the paragraph before this one; here the passage stops adding examples and tells you what kind of place the pool really is.
why.C: The fish from twenty meters down is mentioned only to show it would not last an afternoon in a pool, and nobody in the passage collects or studies it.
why.D: That is the opening, where the pools look peaceful from a distance, and the third paragraph exists to correct that first impression.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The author's attitude toward the animals of the tide pool is best described as

choices.A: amused by how small and helpless the pool creatures are.
choices.B: worried that the pools along the rocky shore will soon disappear.
choices.C: doubtful that they truly survive the changes described.
choices.D: respectful of how well suited they are to a difficult place.

items.explanation: “Equipment, not luck” and “specialists in a kind of hardship” credit the animals with skill instead of pitying them, which rules out the amused reading. Strategy: judge attitude from the author's word choices about the subject, not from the topic alone.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: The passage credits the animals with “equipment, not luck” and calls them specialists, which is the opposite of small and helpless.
why.B: The passage never says the pools are in any danger of disappearing; it is about what the animals living in them can withstand.
why.C: The animals do come through it here, like the barnacle staying damp until the ocean returns, and the author never doubts that.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Home delivery of mail to farmhouses was the most important change of the 1890s.
choices.B: Bicycles could travel over deep, muddy roads more easily than heavy wagons could.
choices.C: Farmers in the 1880s did not care at all what condition their dirt roads were in.
choices.D: A campaign by bicycle riders prepared the roads automobiles would later use.

items.explanation: The passage follows one thread from the riders' Good Roads campaign to the surveys, road departments, and public money that were “already in place” when cars arrived. The choice about mail delivery takes a single step in that chain and inflates it into the whole story. Strategy: a main idea has to account for the final paragraph too.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Mail coming to farmhouses is the step that changed the counties' minds, and the passage does say so. The question asks what the whole passage is about, and it runs from the riders' campaign to the roads cars later used.
why.B: It is the other way round in the passage: the new machines were “almost useless on a rutted road,” while the heavy wagons could grind through whatever the weather left.
why.C: The first paragraph says farmers complained about the ruts; what they resisted was paying for paving out of everyone's taxes.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Post Office require before it would carry letters to a farmhouse?

choices.A: That a local cycling club map and inspect the route first.
choices.B: That the route be one a mail wagon could travel all year.
choices.C: That each farm family pay a small yearly fee for the service.
choices.D: That the road be paved with stone from end to end.

items.explanation: The third paragraph says the Post Office “would only serve routes a mail wagon could travel all year.” The choice about a cycling club mapping the route takes a real detail about the clubs, which mapped the worst stretches, and attaches it to the wrong group. Strategy: match the requirement to the group that actually set it.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Mapping the worst stretches is what the riders' clubs did in their campaign, and the question asks what the Post Office required.
why.C: The passage never has families paying anything for delivery; the one condition named is about the road the mail wagon had to travel.
why.D: The Post Office asked only for a route a mail wagon could travel all year, which is not the same as stone paving from end to end.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: Why did counties that had refused to spend a dollar begin to build roads?

choices.A: A bad road had begun to cost farm families something they wanted.
choices.B: Automobiles had already worn the county's dirt roads down past repair.
choices.C: Farmers had stopped using the heavy wagons that cut ruts in the roads.
choices.D: The cycling clubs had offered to pay for all of the work themselves.

items.explanation: Once a good road was “the difference between getting the mail and not getting it,” paving stopped being a favor to visiting riders and became a local need. The choice about automobiles reverses the passage's order, since cars became common only after these changes. Strategy: look at the sentence just before a result to find its cause.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: The cars come later in the passage: by the time they were common, the surveys and county road departments were already in place.
why.C: The passage never says the heavy wagons stopped; what had to get through all year was the mail wagon.
why.D: The clubs asked state legislatures for the money, which is the very thing the farmers objected to paying for.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: In the second paragraph, *mounted* most nearly means

choices.A: grew steadily larger in size.
choices.B: fastened onto a board or a wall.
choices.C: organized and carried out.
choices.D: climbed up onto something tall.

items.explanation: The clubs “mounted a campaign they called Good Roads,” and the next sentence lists the doing of it: printing pamphlets, mapping stretches, asking legislatures for money. Climbing up onto something is the meaning a reader expects in a passage full of bicycles, but no one climbs onto a campaign. Strategy: let the sentence after the word show which meaning is at work.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Things can mount in that sense, but here the clubs mounted the campaign themselves, and the next sentence lists the doing of it: pamphlets, maps, requests for money.
why.B: That is the meaning for mounting a picture; a campaign of pamphlets and requests to legislatures is not fastened to anything.
why.D: Riders do climb onto bicycles, which is why this meaning feels right in a passage full of them, but nobody climbs onto a campaign.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The sentence “The argument changed when the mail changed” mainly serves to

choices.A: list all of the printed pamphlets and route maps that the cycling clubs produced.
choices.B: repeat the farmers' objection about taxes and city sportsmen in different words.
choices.C: explain the way the mail had been carried to farm families in earlier centuries.
choices.D: mark the point after which paving was no longer dismissed as a favor to city riders.

items.explanation: It stands between the farmers' complaint about city sportsmen and the counties that suddenly began to build, so it announces a switch in reasons. The choice about repeating the objection misses that the sentence overturns the complaint rather than restating it. Strategy: a short sentence set between longer passages usually marks a turn.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: The pamphlets and the maps are listed in the paragraph before; this sentence announces a change rather than adding to that list.
why.B: The objection about taxes and city sportsmen comes just before, and this sentence turns it over instead of saying it again.
why.C: The sentence after this one does say families used to travel to town for their letters, but this short sentence marks the turn in the argument, which is what the question asks about.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: In the last sentence, saying that drivers “owed a debt to people who had been pedaling” means that

choices.A: the author wishes that automobiles had never replaced bicycles at all.
choices.B: drivers benefited from work that cyclists had done for reasons of their own.
choices.C: drivers should have repaid the old cycling clubs with money of their own.
choices.D: cyclists handled the early automobiles better than other people did.

items.explanation: No payment appears anywhere in the passage; the debt is figurative, naming a benefit drivers received from a campaign fought for bicycles. The choice about repaying the clubs with money takes the figure of speech literally, which is the usual trap in this kind of item. Strategy: ask what an image stands for before accepting its literal sense.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: The passage never wishes the automobiles away; it says the drivers owed something to the riders who came first.
why.C: Nobody in the passage ever pays the riders back. The debt is a way of saying drivers got the benefit of work other people had already done.
why.D: The passage never has the cyclists driving anything; their part was the campaign that got smooth roads built.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: What does the scene mainly show about Theo?

choices.A: He realizes that his grandmother left him more work than he could manage.
choices.B: He discovers that he is not suited to selling fruit at a busy market stall.
choices.C: He gives up a rehearsed sales line and lets customers judge the fruit themselves.
choices.D: He learns that neat handwriting matters far more than he had ever thought.

items.explanation: Theo breaks off his practiced sentence, hands over a cherry instead of a description, and by four o’clock the crate is empty. The choice about neat handwriting reverses the ending, in which the hastily written, messier line is the one that works. Strategy: let the final sentence test your choice.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Theo minds the stall for two hours and has time to straighten every plum stem, so the amount of work is not what gets in his way.
why.B: By four o'clock the whole crate of cherries is gone, so the scene ends with him selling them, just not in the way he had practiced.
why.D: Nobody touched the cherries while the neat card was propped up, and the crate emptied after he rewrote a line in handwriting that was not nearly as neat.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: What does Theo do to his price card after the woman buys the cherries?

choices.A: He crosses out a line and adds new words in messier handwriting.
choices.B: He copies the prices onto it from his grandmother’s own list.
choices.C: He throws the card away and writes out a new one from scratch.
choices.D: He props it up against the crate of plums at the end of the table.

items.explanation: The last paragraph says he crossed out one line and wrote underneath “in handwriting that was not nearly as neat.” The choice about propping the card against the plums moves a real detail — the card propped against the scale — to the wrong moment in the scene. Strategy: watch where in the scene each detail happens.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Theo had memorized the prices himself and written them out before the market opened; no list of his grandmother's is mentioned.
why.C: He keeps the card he made. He crosses out one line and writes underneath it.
why.D: He does prop the card up, but against the scale at the start of the morning, and the question asks what he does to it after the woman buys.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The bowl under the table was most likely put there so that

choices.A: Theo could keep count of how many cherries he had sold.
choices.B: Theo’s grandmother would have something to eat later on.
choices.C: bruised cherries could be kept out of the customers’ sight.
choices.D: customers could taste a cherry before buying.

items.explanation: Theo assumes the bowl is her lunch, but it does its work the instant he offers a cherry to the woman, and he then sets it on the table “where people could reach it.” The lunch choice is what the character guesses, not what the scene shows. Strategy: trust what happens in a scene over what a character assumes.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Nothing in the scene uses the bowl for keeping count, and the cherries in it are the ones people get to taste.
why.B: That is what Theo assumes, and the passage adds that his grandmother never ate anything at the market; watch what the bowl actually does when the woman stops.
why.C: The passage never calls any of the cherries bruised; the ones in the bowl are the same cherries as the ones in the crate.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: In the first paragraph, *mind* most nearly means

choices.A: to be bothered by something.
choices.B: to take care of.
choices.C: to hold in his memory.
choices.D: to obey without arguing.

items.explanation: His grandmother leaves and “for two hours the stall was his to mind,” so he is the one looking after it. Being bothered by something is the meaning most readers meet first, as in “I don’t mind,” but a stall cannot be bothered by anybody. Strategy: substitute each choice into the sentence and hear which one survives.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: That is the meaning when you say you do not mind something, but a fruit stall cannot be bothered by anything; the stall was his to look after.
why.C: Theo did memorize the prices, which makes this meaning feel close, but the thing that was his for two hours was the stall itself.
why.D: The word can mean obeying a person, and here what he minds is a stall, which nobody obeys.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The dash in “They’re excellent for—” marks the point at which

choices.A: Theo abandons the sentence he practiced and changes his approach.
choices.B: Theo’s grandmother comes back to the stall with the change.
choices.C: the woman in the yellow coat interrupts Theo with another question.
choices.D: Theo forgets the prices he had memorized before the market opened.

items.explanation: The narrator says he stopped “because he could hear how it sounded: like a boy repeating something,” and from there he shows the fruit instead of describing it. The choice about an interruption gives the woman credit for a decision Theo makes on his own. Strategy: punctuation that breaks a sentence often marks the turn of a scene.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: His grandmother has gone to find change and does not come back anywhere in the scene; Theo is the one who stops the sentence.
why.C: The woman had already asked her question, and the passage says he stopped because he could hear how it sounded.
why.D: The prices are not the trouble. He stops because the practiced sentence sounded “like a boy repeating something.”

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The last sentence, about the empty crate and the beautifully arranged plums, is best described as

choices.A: wistful and sad about the end of a long day at the market.
choices.B: quietly amused, setting what looked good beside what actually sold.
choices.C: excited and boastful about how much money Theo managed to earn.
choices.D: sharply critical of the mistakes Theo made over the course of the day.

items.explanation: The plums are called “arranged so beautifully” at the exact moment we learn they did not sell, a small joke the narrator makes without scolding Theo. Reading the line as sharp criticism mistakes gentle humor for blame. Strategy: notice when a detail from the opening returns with its meaning changed.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Nothing in the sentence sounds sorry, and an empty crate is good news at a market stall.
why.C: No money and no total appear at the end, and the sentence is quiet rather than boastful.
why.D: The narrator is gentle here: the joke is that the beautifully arranged plums are the ones still sitting there, and it is not aimed at Theo.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: A damper is the only device that keeps a very tall tower standing up.
choices.B: Strong wind is the greatest danger that any tall building will ever face.
choices.C: A building that moves at all in the wind has been built incorrectly.
choices.D: A tall building is built to sway a little and then stop quickly.

items.explanation: The passage first explains why a frame is given room to bend and then why engineers work to make the motion fade fast, ending with what they actually measure. The choice naming the damper treats one device as the entire design and ignores the frame's give. Strategy: a main idea must hold both halves of a two-part explanation.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: The damper is the answer to one problem, the swaying that lingers, and the frame's measured give comes before it; the question asks what the whole passage is about.
why.B: The passage never ranks the dangers a tall building faces. It explains what engineers do about wind.
why.C: The first paragraph says the movement “is not a flaw” and that engineers planned it.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: According to the passage, where is a damper placed in a tower?

choices.A: Inside the outer wall on every floor from top to bottom.
choices.B: Beside the scale model inside the engineers' wind tunnel.
choices.C: High in the building, on cables or on a slick steel surface.
choices.D: Below the ground floor, deep inside the building's foundation.

items.explanation: The third paragraph describes an enormous weight “hung high in the building on cables or resting on a slick steel surface.” The wind tunnel choice reuses the final paragraph, where models, not dampers, are placed. Strategy: reread the sentence that names the thing the question asks about.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: The damper in the passage is one enormous weight, not something spread through the walls floor by floor.
why.B: The wind tunnel in the last paragraph holds a model, and the question asks where a damper sits in a real tower.
why.D: The passage hangs the weight high in the building, which is the opposite end from the foundation.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The passage suggests that a damper is added mainly to

choices.A: make a building that is already safe feel steadier to the people inside.
choices.B: keep the building from moving at all, even during the hardest storm.
choices.C: make the steel frame far stiffer than it would otherwise have been.
choices.D: lower the cost of putting up a tall tower in a crowded city.

items.explanation: The paragraph says long swaying “feels alarming to the people inside it, even when it is perfectly safe,” and the damper is introduced as the answer to that problem. The choice about stopping all motion ignores “the sway fades in seconds instead of minutes,” which shortens the movement rather than ending it. Strategy: notice the exact problem a device is introduced to solve.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: The passage says the sway “fades in seconds instead of minutes,” so the movement is shortened rather than stopped.
why.C: Stiffness is the thing the passage warns about, because wind pressing on a rigid wall has nowhere to send its force; the damper does not stiffen the frame.
why.D: Cost never comes up for the damper. The only cost the passage names is the hidden one in building a tower too stiff.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: In the second paragraph, *give* most nearly means

choices.A: a willingness to share things with others.
choices.B: a sudden collapse under a heavy weight.
choices.C: a present that is offered without charge.
choices.D: the ability to bend and spring back.

items.explanation: The frame built with “a measured amount of give” bends, sheds the energy of the gust, and “returns to where it started.” The sudden-collapse choice is tempting because a beam can “give way,” but this frame comes back rather than failing. Strategy: read one sentence past the word before choosing.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: That is the meaning tied to giving things away, and a steel frame is not sharing anything.
why.B: A beam can give way, which is why this meaning feels close, but this frame bends, sheds the energy of the gust, and “returns to where it started.”
why.C: That is a present; here the word names what the frame does in the wind, bending a little and springing back.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The sentence “The harder problem is not the leaning but the lingering” mainly serves to

choices.A: give an example of a tall tower that was damaged in a winter storm.
choices.B: shift the discussion from why buildings bend to how the motion stops.
choices.C: introduce an objection that the author goes on to reject in detail.
choices.D: restate the point of the opening paragraph in stronger, plainer language.

items.explanation: Everything before it explains bending; everything after it explains the damper that shortens the sway. Calling it an objection fails, because the author agrees with the sentence and builds on it instead of answering it. Strategy: read the sentences on both sides to see what a hinge sentence separates.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: The passage never names a tower that a storm damaged, and this sentence is pointing ahead to the next problem rather than giving an example.
why.C: The author agrees with this sentence and spends the rest of the paragraph on the lingering it names.
why.D: The opening paragraph is about the leaning, and this sentence sets the leaning aside to raise something new: how long the swaying lasts.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The last three sentences (“In a wind tunnel … how quickly it stops.”) create a tone of

choices.A: doubt about whether wind tunnel tests are worth the trouble.
choices.B: quiet confidence about what the engineers already know.
choices.C: alarm at how far a tall building moves during a storm.
choices.D: impatience with engineers who measure too many things.

items.explanation: The short, flat sentences — “They already know it will” — present the movement as settled fact rather than a surprise or a worry. Alarm is the reaction the whole passage argues against, beginning with “it is not a flaw.” Strategy: read a passage's closing lines for the author's settled position.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: The engineers in these lines are measuring exactly what they mean to measure, and nothing suggests the test is not worth doing.
why.C: Alarm is what the whole passage argues against, starting with the movement being “a few centimeters at most” and “not a flaw.”
why.D: These lines narrow the test to one thing, how quickly the motion stops, and the passage has no complaint about that.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The passage is mainly written to

choices.A: prove that repairing a broken object always costs a school less money than replacing it with a new one.
choices.B: describe the objects that the Thursday repair table at Fenwick Middle School brought back in its first term.
choices.C: explain why building projects such as birdhouses and model bridges should be removed from schools entirely.
choices.D: argue that schools should set aside regular time for repair, because repairing teaches careful attention.

items.explanation: The author asks for “one bench, one box of tools, and one period a week for repair” and says the point of the hour “is to teach a habit of looking.” The choice about the Fenwick table names one supporting example, and the choice about saving money is contradicted by the author's own words that the point “is not to save the school money on chairs.” Strategy: choose the choice that covers the whole argument, not one example.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: The author never claims repair is cheaper — he says outright that the point of the hour "is not to save the school money on chairs."
why.B: The passage really does list those forty-one items, but Fenwick is one example offered as support; the question asks what the whole passage is written to do.
why.C: Birdhouses and model bridges are in the first paragraph, but the author asks for repair to be added, not for building to be taken away.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Thursday repair table bring back during its first term?

choices.A: Forty-one items, every one of them either a lamp or an umbrella.
choices.B: Forty-one items, including eleven lamps and fifteen damaged library books.
choices.C: Four items, one for each of the four students who stayed until June.
choices.D: Fifteen backpacks and nine library books with badly broken spines.

items.explanation: The passage lists forty-one items: eleven lamps, nine backpacks, six umbrellas, and fifteen library books with broken spines. The choice naming four items confuses the four long-term students with the count of objects, and the backpacks-and-books choice swaps those two numbers. Strategy: put your finger on the exact sentence before choosing.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: The forty-one is right, but the same list also gives nine backpacks and fifteen library books, so lamps and umbrellas are only part of it.
why.C: Four is a real number from that paragraph, but it counts the students still at the table in June, not the things they mended.
why.D: Those two numbers have traded places: the passage gives nine backpacks and fifteen library books with broken spines.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The author would most likely say that a school's repair period is working well when

choices.A: the school spends far less money on new furniture than it did the year before.
choices.B: every broken object brought to the bench is successfully fixed by a student.
choices.C: students finish their repairs faster than a paid repair shop nearby would.
choices.D: students keep coming back after the first excitement and show newcomers what they know.

items.explanation: The author calls four the number worth watching — the students still at the table in June, “showing newcomers how to seat a screw” — so a lasting habit and passed-on skill are the real measure. The choice about furniture savings is ruled out by “not to save the school money,” and the choice about fixing everything by the admission that “some objects truly cannot be mended.” Strategy: infer from what the author calls important, not from what sounds sensible in general.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: The author sets this measure aside himself — the point of the hour "is not to save the school money on chairs."
why.B: The last paragraph says plainly that some objects truly cannot be mended, so fixing everything could not be the author's test of success.
why.C: The author admits repairing is slower than replacing and answers that objection rather than promising speed — and no repair shop appears in the passage at all.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: As used in the second paragraph, “sound” most nearly means

choices.A: making a loud noise.
choices.B: sturdy and undamaged.
choices.C: cheap and easy to replace.

why.A: That is how the cardinal's red is made, and the passage offers it as the opposite case to the jay, not as the rule for both birds.

why.B: The passage mentions hauling the blocks but never says the large size made carrying them any easier.
why.C: The passage does say the blocks were hauled some distance, but the reason it gives for cutting them large is about how slowly stored ice melts, not about the trip.

choices.C: Leaving wide gaps between the blocks so air can circulate.

why.A: Smaller pieces have more surface for the same amount of ice, and surface is exactly what sets the pace of melting.
why.C: Workers did the opposite, stacking the blocks tight and filling the seams so little ice was left in the open.

The bags do thump onto the quilt later, but that thumping is never offered as a reason for choosing the spot. Strategy: when the passage gives a reason in the word because, take that one and stop hunting.

why.A: This sounds like a sensible reason for practicing over a bed, but the passage never mentions the floor below or gives noise as the reason for the spot.
why.C: This sounds sensible for juggling, but the passage says nothing about the height of the room.
why.D: The room is Neel's and no one else appears in it, but the passage gives a different reason outright.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: The Moon does not spin at all, which is why one face always points at us.
choices.B: The Moon's far side was first photographed by a spacecraft that flew behind it.
choices.C: The half we never see is permanently dark, unlike the half that faces Earth.
choices.D: Earth's pull settled the Moon into a spin that matches its orbit.

items.explanation: The passage sets up a puzzle in the first paragraph (the Moon must turn once per lap to keep one face toward us) and spends the third paragraph explaining what put it into that rhythm. The choice about the 1959 spacecraft is true but is a single closing detail, and the choice about a permanently dark half is contradicted in the last paragraph. Strategy: the main idea has to cover the whole passage, not one sentence of it.

why.A: This is the exact guess the first paragraph calls the reverse of the truth, so it is the idea the passage sets out to correct.
why.B: That happens in the very last sentence, and one closing fact is far too small to be what the whole passage is about.
why.C: The passage says outright that the hidden half gets as much sunlight as the half we know.

choices.B: It is going through its night.
choices.C: It is turned toward the Sun.
choices.D: It is warmer than the near side.

items.explanation: The last paragraph states it directly: when the Moon looks full to us, the far side is in night. The choice about lasting darkness borrows the name people use for that half, which is the very name the paragraph calls wrong. Strategy: for a detail question, find the sentence that mentions the thing the question names, and read it all the way to the end.

why.A: This is the dark-side idea the paragraph is written to correct, since the far side gets as much sunlight as the half we know.
why.C: A full Moon means our side is the lit one, so the far side is the side facing away from the sunlight just then.
why.D: The passage never compares the two halves for warmth. It says only which one is in night.

items.prompt: The passage suggests that if the Moon's orbit were a perfect circle,

choices.A: the Moon would stop turning on its axis.
choices.B: the far side would get sunlight of its own.
choices.C: observers would have less of the Moon to chart.
choices.D: the Moon would need much longer to finish a lap.

items.explanation: The thin strip of the far side that observers managed to chart comes from the rocking, and the rocking comes from the Moon hurrying and lagging in an orbit that is not a true circle. Take the uneven orbit away and that strip goes with it, so there would be less of the Moon to map than the little-more-than-half they reached. Strategy: when a question removes a cause, follow the chain the passage already built and ask which effect shrinks.

why.A: Nothing in the passage ties the shape of the orbit to whether the Moon turns. The spin was settled long ago by the bulge.
why.B: The far side already gets as much sunlight as the near side, so a rounder orbit would change nothing about that.
why.D: The passage says the orbit's shape makes the Moon hurry and lag along the way, not that it changes how long a lap takes.

choices.D: lacking courage or firmness.

items.explanation: The bulge is the small stretch that Earth's slightly stronger pull produces, so faint here means barely there, hardly noticeable. The dizzy and the quiet-sound meanings are both genuine senses of the word, which is what makes them tempting, but neither fits a shape in rock. Strategy: read each meaning back into the actual sentence and keep the one that still makes sense.

why.B: That is a real meaning of the word, but rock does not feel dizzy, and the sentence is describing a shape.
why.C: A bulge is something you could see or measure, not something that makes a sound.
why.D: This meaning turns up in words like faint-hearted, and nothing in a stretched piece of rock is being called cowardly.

items.prompt: The second paragraph mainly serves to

choices.A: let the reader act out the Moon's once-per-lap turn.
choices.B: introduce the gravity explained in the paragraph after it.
choices.C: prove that a chair and a moon obey the same laws.
choices.D: show that the Moon's motion is too odd to picture.

items.explanation: The first paragraph makes a claim that sounds wrong at first hearing, and the chair paragraph hands the reader a way to perform that same turn and feel that it is true. It introduces no new cause and it argues nothing about laws. Strategy: ask what a short paragraph does for the paragraph before it, not just what objects it mentions.

why.B: Gravity does not appear anywhere in the chair paragraph; it arrives fresh at the start of the next one.
why.C: The paragraph asks the reader to walk one circle, and nothing more. It never claims that a chair and a moon are governed by the same laws, which would be a far larger claim than this passage makes anywhere.
why.D: The paragraph does the opposite, making the motion easy to picture by putting the reader inside it.

items.prompt: In saying that the same dark patches *stare back*, the author suggests that

choices.A: the Moon is keeping watch over Earth.
choices.B: the same view meets us each time.
choices.C: the dark patches slowly change shape.
choices.D: the patches are hard to see clearly.

items.explanation: Patches of rock cannot stare, so the phrase has to mean something else, and the two words before it say what: tonight, and again next month, the same ones. It is a way of saying the view never changes. Strategy: when a writer gives an object a human action, ask what the action is standing in for, and look at the words around it for the answer.

why.A: This takes the staring literally. The patches are markings, and the author is describing what we see, not something the Moon is doing on purpose.
why.C: The whole point of the sentence is that the patches do not change, which is what makes the rest of the passage surprising.
why.D: The patches are the part that is easy to see; the passage never says anything about how hard they are to make out.

items.prompt: The author's main purpose in this passage is to

choices.A: explain why the grade of Hill Street is gentler at the park gate than at the top.
choices.B: argue that Hill Street needs benches back and that the town must keep them up.
choices.C: describe how one neighbor has done her shopping on foot for the past fifty years.
choices.D: persuade neighbors to take turns driving Ruth up the hill to the grocery store.

items.explanation: The first paragraph makes the request — benches back on Hill Street, spaced so that nobody climbs a whole block without a stop — and the third paragraph adds the other half of it, that the washing and the painting come out of the same budget as the benches. Everything else supports that request: the slope sets it up, Ruth shows what a bench does, the ending says what is at stake. Strategy: the main idea has to account for the whole argument, including the part about upkeep.

why.A: The slope is described in the opening lines, but it is the setting for the argument rather than the thing the author is asking the town to do.
why.C: Ruth is one example used to support the request, and a main idea has to cover the whole passage, not a single person inside it.
why.D: The car does appear in the passage, but the author is addressing the town and asking for benches, not organizing rides for anybody.

items.prompt: According to the passage, what did Ruth do while the bench outside the bakery was still there?

choices.A: She had her groceries brought to her by car on Tuesdays.
choices.B: She walked up on Tuesdays and carried her shopping down.
choices.C: She waited at the bench for someone to drive her up the hill.
choices.D: She carried her shopping up the hill and walked back down.

items.explanation: One sentence in the second paragraph answers this directly: while the bench stood outside the bakery, she walked up on Tuesdays and carried her shopping down. Strategy: when a passage describes a before and an after, put your finger on which one the question asks about, then check the direction of travel.

why.A: That is what happens now that the bench is gone, so this choice puts the after-picture into the before-slot.
why.C: Nobody in the passage waits at the bench for a ride; the bench is a place to stop partway through her own climb.
why.D: Every piece of this is in the sentence, but the trip runs the other way: she walked up and carried the shopping down.

items.prompt: Suppose the town offered to install twelve benches but would not pay to wash or repaint them. Based on the passage, the author would most likely

choices.A: prefer six benches the town has promised to look after.
choices.B: accept the twelve, since more places to stop is the goal.
choices.C: ask that the money go toward widening the sidewalk instead.
choices.D: agree, if neighbors themselves did the washing and painting.

items.explanation: The author has already faced this exact trade. There is room on Hill Street for twelve, and the author asks for six anyway, on the grounds that benches nobody looks after splinter before long — so a smaller number with the upkeep attached is the deal the author chose once cost was the objection. Strategy: when a question invents a new situation, look for the place where the author has already made the same choice.

why.B: More benches sounds like more of what the author wants, but the author says plainly that the ask is six with upkeep, even though twelve would fit on the street.
why.C: A wider sidewalk was the town's own answer last time, and the second paragraph exists to say that a bench does what widening cannot.
why.D: The author asks for the upkeep to come out of the town's budget, and nowhere offers to take that work on.

why.B: A street does not have school years, and the sentence is comparing the bottom of the hill with the top.
why.C: The word can describe how good a material is, but here gentle and steep are describing a slope, not a quality.

choices.A: restate the cost of upkeep that the third paragraph accepts.
choices.B: recall how Ruth used the bench outside the bakery.
choices.C: admit what benches cannot do and name what they decide.

items.explanation: Having said what a bench does, the author closes by giving one thing up and claiming another: the hill will stay exactly as steep as it was, and the benches will settle who is able to walk up it. why.A: The cost of keeping benches up is granted in the paragraph before this one, and the closing lines never return to it.
why.B: Ruth's Tuesdays belong to the second paragraph, and the ending does not go back to her.
why.D: The author never counts users; the last line is about who is able to climb the hill, not how many will sit down.

items.prompt: In the last paragraph the author calls a sidewalk with benches “a room” in order to suggest that

choices.D: a bench can make a public sidewalk feel like part of a home.

items.explanation: A corridor is somewhere you walk through on your way elsewhere, and the author sets it against a room, then says straight out that people stay in rooms and offers two small pictures of staying. Strategy: when an author makes a comparison, read the sentence just after it, which usually tells you what the comparison is for.

why.B: The passage does compare a bench to a small building, but that comparison is about upkeep, not about how much room a bench fills.
why.C: Nobody is asking for a roof here; the room is a way of describing the sidewalk, not a thing to be built on top of it.
why.D: A room does suggest a house, but the contrast the author draws is corridor against room — passing through against staying — not public against private.
